teaches: Choosing a microphone type for the source

Why two microphones can cancel each other

nodes.label: Synthesis
nodes.blurb: Sound built from nothing: an oscillator makes the raw tone, then filters and envelopes shape it into something playable
teaches: What each waveform's harmonics sound like

How an envelope gives a sound its shape
Using an LFO to put movement in

nodes.label: Sampling
nodes.blurb: Recorded sound as raw material: crop it, stretch it, reverse it, and it becomes an instrument you never played

Warping a sample to the project tempo

nodes.label: Sequencing
nodes.blurb: MIDI carries instructions, not sound, which is why a sequenced part can be re-timed, re-voiced and corrected long after you played it
teaches: Recording in real time or step by step
What quantise fixes and what it flattens
Editing velocity and note length for feel

nodes.label: Audio Editing
nodes.blurb: Where one good take gets assembled out of several imperfect ones, quietly enough that nobody hears the joins

nodes.label: Pitch and Rhythm Correction
nodes.blurb: Correction is a judgement, not a button: how far you pull a performance toward the grid changes what it sounds like
teaches: Tuning without losing the singer's formants
Choosing a warp mode to suit the material
Quantising rhythm while keeping the groove
Working offline against working in real time

nodes.label: Automation
nodes.blurb: Automation is the mix moving: a level, a filter or a send that changes over time so the arrangement keeps developing
teaches: Writing volume and pan moves over time
Automating an effect rather than a level
Choosing curve shapes for smooth changes
Editing breakpoints and clip envelopes

nodes.label: Dynamic Processing

teaches: Setting threshold and ratio for the source

Reading a compression or gating graph

nodes.label: Stereo
nodes.blurb: Two speakers, one image: stereo is built from timing and level differences that your ears read as direction and width
teaches: Choosing a stereo microphone pair for the room
Panning to place a sound, not just to spread it

Using the Haas effect deliberately

nodes.label: EQ
nodes.blurb: EQ is subtraction as often as addition: you make room for one sound by taking frequencies out of another
teaches: Shelves, bands and high-pass filters
What Q actually changes
Sweeping to find a problem frequency
Clearing sibilance, hum and rumble

nodes.label: Delay
nodes.blurb: A repeat you can place in time, long enough to hear as an echo, short enough to stop being one and become a tone
teaches: Syncing repeats to the project tempo

Slapback, ping-pong and multi-tap in use

nodes.label: Reverb
nodes.blurb: The room you did not record in: its size, its surfaces, and how long it takes for the sound to disappear
teaches: Pre-delay, decay and damping in practice
Algorithmic against convolution reverb

nodes.label: Modulation
nodes.blurb: A parameter moving on its own: one LFO sits behind chorus, flanging, phasing and tremolo alike
teaches: How rate, depth and waveform change the effect
What separates chorus, flanger and phaser
Tremolo against vibrato: level or pitch
Ring modulation's carrier and modulator

nodes.label: Distortion
nodes.blurb: Controlled damage: clipping a waveform adds harmonics that were never in the original sound
teaches: Overdrive, fuzz, saturation and bitcrushing
Hard clipping against soft clipping
Why symmetry decides which harmonics appear
Keeping gain staging under control

nodes.blurb: The mix before the effects: faders, panning and space arranged so every part can be heard without fighting
teaches: Building a static mix first

nodes.label: Mastering

teaches: Loudness targets and true peak limits

Preparing files for each delivery format

nodes.label: Acoustics

nodes.label: Monitor Speakers

teaches: Balanced against unbalanced connections
Reading TRS, TS and XLR wiring

When a DI box is the right answer

nodes.label: Digital Analogue

teaches: What sample rate and bit depth each decide

How aliasing appears, and how to avoid it
What analogue still does differently

nodes.label: Numeracy
nodes.blurb: The working-out the exam asks for: delay times, dynamic range, gain changes, each one answering a practical studio question
teaches: Working out delay times from tempo
Moving between octaves, semitones and cents
Reading the decibel scale and its ratios
Checking a sample rate against Nyquist

nodes.label: Levels
nodes.blurb: Level is the one thing every stage shares: set it wrong early and no amount of later processing fully recovers it

Gain staging through the whole chain
Staying clear of clipping and the noise floor

nodes.label: DAW software
nodes.blurb: Ableton Live, Logic Pro and Pro Tools bundle multi-track recording, MIDI sequencing and mixing in one environment.

nodes.label: Audio interfaces
nodes.blurb: An interface's ADC and DAC bridge analogue and digital audio, connecting studio hardware to a computer.

nodes.label: Sample rate and bit depth
nodes.blurb: Higher sample rates and bit depths capture more audio detail but increase file size and processing demand.

nodes.label: MIDI controllers
nodes.blurb: Keyboard controllers, drum pads and control surfaces feed MIDI data into a DAW for real-time performance and automation.

nodes.label: Plug-in formats
nodes.blurb: VST, AU and AAX plug-ins host virtual instruments and effects inside a DAW.

nodes.label: System requirements
nodes.blurb: CPU speed, RAM and SSD storage determine how many tracks and plug-ins a system can run without dropouts.

nodes.label: Drivers (ASIO/Core Audio)
nodes.blurb: ASIO on Windows and Core Audio on macOS are low-latency driver protocols essential for professional monitoring.

nodes.label: Buffer size and latency
nodes.blurb: Smaller buffer sizes cut monitoring latency but raise CPU demand, risking audio dropouts during recording.

nodes.label: Connector types
nodes.blurb: XLR, TRS, TS, MIDI, USB and optical connectors each suit a different signal type.

nodes.label: Studio hardware components
nodes.blurb: Microphones, mixing consoles, monitors and outboard equipment each occupy a stage in the signal chain.
nodes.family: Hardware components in a studio setup

nodes.label: DI boxes
nodes.blurb: A DI box converts a high-impedance instrument signal to balanced low-impedance, letting guitars feed a mixing desk cleanly.
nodes.family: Hardware components in a studio setup

nodes.label: Signal chain
nodes.blurb: Signal chain traces the path from source through processing to output, often tested in exam questions.
nodes.family: Hardware components in a studio setup

nodes.label: Gain structure
nodes.blurb: Setting gain so peaks sit around -6 to -12 dBFS maximises signal-to-noise ratio while avoiding clipping.
nodes.family: Gain structure and how it affects noise and distortion

nodes.label: Pre-amp controls
nodes.blurb: Phantom power, pad, high-pass filter and polarity switches on a pre-amp shape the signal before recording.
nodes.family: Gain structure and how it affects noise and distortion

nodes.label: Microphone types
nodes.blurb: Dynamic, condenser and ribbon microphones differ in sensitivity and durability, so the source determines which type suits best.
nodes.family: Characteristics and suitability of microphone types

nodes.label: Microphone placement
nodes.blurb: Distance and angle from a source change captured tone and level, guiding placement choices for each instrument.

nodes.label: Multi-microphone recording
nodes.blurb: Recording a drum kit with several microphones needs careful spacing to avoid phase cancellation between capsules.

nodes.label: On-axis and off-axis response
nodes.blurb: A microphone's frequency response changes off-axis, so angling it away from a source tames harsh highs.

nodes.label: Polar patterns
nodes.blurb: Cardioid, hypercardioid, figure-of-eight and omnidirectional patterns each reject sound differently, affecting isolation and background bleed.
nodes.family: Advantages and disadvantages of polar pattern and frequency response

nodes.label: Proximity effect
nodes.blurb: Directional microphones boost bass as a source moves closer, an effect entirely absent from omnidirectional designs.
nodes.family: Advantages and disadvantages of polar pattern and frequency response

nodes.label: Frequency and transient response
nodes.blurb: A microphone's frequency and transient response determine how accurately it captures tone and fast-changing sounds.
nodes.family: Advantages and disadvantages of polar pattern and frequency response

nodes.label: Phase relationships
nodes.blurb: Combining multiple microphones on one source can cause phase cancellation, so engineers manage timing differences between capsules carefully.

nodes.label: Stereo mic techniques
nodes.blurb: Coincident and spaced stereo pairs capture width differently, trading phase accuracy for a wider, more diffuse stereo image.

nodes.label: How microphones work
nodes.blurb: Electromagnetic induction drives moving-coil dynamics while capacitance between charged plates drives condensers, giving each its character.

nodes.label: Phantom power
nodes.blurb: Condenser microphones need +48V phantom power to charge their capsule, but it can damage a passive ribbon mic.

nodes.label: Microphone accessories
nodes.blurb: Pop shields and elastic suspension cradles reduce plosives and mechanical vibration from reaching the capsule during recording.

nodes.label: Waveforms
nodes.blurb: Sine, square, sawtooth and triangle waveforms each carry different harmonic content, giving synthesis its raw tonal starting point.

nodes.label: Harmonic content
nodes.blurb: A waveform's harmonic content shapes its timbre: sawtooth contains all harmonics, the usual start for subtractive synthesis.

nodes.label: Octave relationships
nodes.blurb: Each octave doubles a waveform's fundamental frequency, a relationship students must apply in pitch and frequency calculations.

nodes.label: Low-pass filter
nodes.blurb: A low-pass filter removes frequencies above the cutoff, producing a darker, warmer tone than the source.

nodes.label: High-pass and band-pass filters
nodes.blurb: High-pass filters thin a sound by removing bass, while band-pass filters isolate a narrow range between two cutoffs.

nodes.label: Resonance (Q)
nodes.blurb: Resonance boosts the signal right at the cutoff frequency, and extreme settings can push the filter into self-oscillation.

nodes.label: ADSR envelope
nodes.blurb: Attack, Decay, Sustain and Release shape amplitude over time; Sustain alone is a level, not a duration.

nodes.label: LFO modulation
nodes.blurb: An LFO cycles below audible range to modulate pitch, filter cutoff or amplitude, creating vibrato, wah or tremolo.

nodes.label: LFO rate and depth
nodes.blurb: Rate sets how fast an LFO cycles while depth sets how strongly it affects its target.

nodes.label: FM synthesis
nodes.blurb: FM synthesis uses one oscillator to modulate another's frequency, producing complex timbres beyond simple subtractive shaping.

nodes.label: Carrier and modulator
nodes.blurb: In FM synthesis the carrier produces the audible tone while the modulator alters it, creating complex timbres.

nodes.label: Spectrum analysis
nodes.blurb: Spectrum analysers visually confirm a synthesised sound's harmonic content, helping students verify pitch and timbre accuracy.

nodes.label: Octave matching
nodes.blurb: Octave matching means tuning a synthesised sound to a specified pitch, a skill students often find challenging.

nodes.label: Frequency and pitch maths
nodes.blurb: A4 equals 440 Hz and each octave doubles that frequency, underpinning cents, semitones and harmonic series calculations.

nodes.label: Breakbeat sampling
nodes.blurb: Extracting and isolating drum breaks from recordings supplies rhythmic material that students then crop, loop and rearrange.

nodes.label: Vocal sampling
nodes.blurb: Capturing and processing vocal elements turns spoken or sung phrases into reusable musical or textural material.

nodes.label: Instrument sampling
nodes.blurb: Recording acoustic or electric instruments as samples lets a producer manipulate performances that would be hard to replay.

nodes.label: Environmental sampling
nodes.blurb: Field recordings of real-world sound feed sound-design and creative sampling projects beyond conventional musical sources.

nodes.label: Sample clearance and copyright
nodes.blurb: Using another artist's recording without clearance can breach copyright, so commercial release depends on understanding fair use rules.

nodes.label: Cropping and editing
nodes.blurb: Setting precise start and end points isolates exactly the material needed and removes unwanted noise from a sample.

nodes.label: Pitch manipulation
nodes.blurb: Transposing a sample up or down changes its pitch, and can be done with or without affecting tempo.

nodes.label: Time-stretching
nodes.blurb: Time-stretching changes a sample's duration without altering its pitch, using a warp algorithm suited to the source material.

nodes.label: Reverse and speed change
nodes.blurb: Reversing a sample creates a backward texture, while changing playback speed shifts pitch and timing together.

nodes.label: Glitched vocals
nodes.blurb: Deliberate digital artefacts and stutter effects turn a clean vocal sample into a rhythmic or textural glitch effect.

nodes.label: Layering techniques
nodes.blurb: Combining multiple samples builds denser, more complex textures than any single source could produce alone.

nodes.label: Chopping and rearranging
nodes.blurb: Breaking a sample into segments and reordering them reconstructs new rhythms or melodies from existing material.

nodes.label: Granular manipulation
nodes.blurb: Granular techniques micro-edit a sample into tiny grains, creating textures far removed from the original recording.

nodes.label: Warp markers
nodes.blurb: Warp markers lock sample playback to the project tempo, keeping timing synchronised across an arrangement.

nodes.label: Real-time input
nodes.blurb: Playing a MIDI controller keyboard live captures natural timing and velocity directly into the sequencer.

nodes.label: Step input
nodes.blurb: A step grid or pencil tool lets a producer draw in notes precisely, without performing them live.

nodes.label: Quantise values
nodes.blurb: Hard quantise snaps notes to values like 8, 16 or 32, correcting timing but removing all human feel.

nodes.label: Swing quantise
nodes.blurb: Swing or percentage quantise displaces alternate grid positions, adding deliberate groove rather than perfectly even timing.

nodes.label: Snap and grid
nodes.blurb: Snap-to-grid settings constrain note placement during editing, making precise timing easier to achieve by eye.

nodes.label: Velocity and note length
nodes.blurb: Velocity controls how hard a note is struck while note length controls staccato versus legato phrasing.

nodes.label: Piano roll and list editor
nodes.blurb: The piano roll shows notes visually against a timeline, while the list editor shows the same data numerically.

nodes.label: Cutting, looping and duplicating
nodes.blurb: Cutting, looping and duplicating MIDI regions builds arrangements quickly from a small amount of recorded or programmed material.

nodes.label: MIDI data bytes
nodes.blurb: MIDI messages send note on/off, pitch and controller data as bytes rather than audio.

nodes.label: Pitch bend
nodes.blurb: Pitch bend uses two data bytes for 14-bit resolution, giving smooth pitch changes without audible stepping.

nodes.label: LSB and MSB
nodes.blurb: Least and Most Significant Bytes combine to encode high-resolution values like pitch bend data.

nodes.label: Tempo data
nodes.blurb: Tempo is stored as bpm data, letting a sequence hold a fixed tempo or change over time.

nodes.label: Destructive vs non-destructive editing
nodes.blurb: Non-destructive editing preserves the original file and allows unlimited revision, unlike destructive editing which permanently alters it.

nodes.label: Comping
nodes.blurb: Comping assembles the best sections from multiple takes into one track, judged on timing, tone and performance.

nodes.label: Cut, copy & paste
nodes.blurb: Cutting, copying and pasting audio regions at precise bar positions is the most examined practical editing task.

nodes.label: Zero-crossing edits
nodes.blurb: Placing edit points where the waveform crosses zero amplitude prevents the clicks caused by mid-wave cuts.

nodes.label: Fades & crossfades
nodes.blurb: A short 5–15ms crossfade at every edit boundary eliminates clicks; missing one is the most common exam error.

nodes.label: Noise & artefact removal
nodes.blurb: Silence removes unwanted noise or breaths without shifting timing, unlike delete, which drags everything after it forward.

nodes.label: Pitch-shifting
nodes.blurb: Pitch-shifting changes an audio region's pitch without affecting duration, preserving formants to keep the timbre natural.

nodes.label: Audio quantisation
nodes.blurb: Audio quantisation automatically aligns recorded transients to the musical grid, useful for tightening multi-mic drum recordings.

nodes.label: Multi-section arrangement
nodes.blurb: Copying and pasting multi-bar sections must land on the correct bar range with no gaps or doubling.

nodes.label: Consolidation & bounce
nodes.blurb: Consolidating merges multiple edits into one file, and bouncing in place renders virtual edits as permanent audio.

nodes.label: Spectrum analysis & tuner
nodes.blurb: Spectrum analysers and tuners visually identify pitch deviation in cents before any transposition is applied.

nodes.label: Transposition & fine-tuning
nodes.blurb: Transposition shifts pitch by semitones, while fine-tuning in cents (100 per semitone) corrects small deviations precisely.

nodes.label: Formant preservation
nodes.blurb: Formant preservation keeps a voice's natural timbre intact while its pitch is shifted up or down.

nodes.label: Rhythm quantisation
nodes.blurb: Quantisation automatically aligns recorded transients to the musical grid, though over-quantising can remove natural human feel.

nodes.label: Tempo mapping
nodes.blurb: Tempo mapping matches a recording's tempo to the DAW project so warp-based correction stays in time.

nodes.label: Groove templates
nodes.blurb: Groove templates apply a specific rhythmic feel, such as swing, to quantised audio for a musical result.

nodes.label: Warp modes
nodes.blurb: Complex Pro gives the highest-quality pitch correction for vocals; Beats mode suits percussive material only, not vocals.

nodes.label: Re-Pitch mode
nodes.blurb: Re-Pitch links pitch to playback speed like analogue tape, so it cannot correct pitch independently of timing.

nodes.label: Real-time vs offline correction
nodes.blurb: Real-time correction processes pitch live during performance, while offline correction allows more precise, considered adjustment afterwards.

nodes.label: Volume automation
nodes.blurb: Volume automation rides a track's level over time, keeping vocals consistent or shaping dynamic contrast.

nodes.label: Panning automation
nodes.blurb: Panning automation moves a signal across the stereo field over time, creating width or spatial storytelling.

nodes.label: Send automation
nodes.blurb: Send automation varies how much signal reaches a reverb or delay return, changing spatial depth over time.

nodes.label: Effect parameter automation
nodes.blurb: Automating EQ, compression or delay parameters lets effects change dynamically instead of staying fixed throughout a track.

nodes.label: Automation curve types
nodes.blurb: Linear automation moves in a straight line; curved automation transitions smoothly; step automation jumps abruptly for rhythm.

nodes.label: LFO automation
nodes.blurb: LFO automation uses a cyclical low-frequency oscillator to modulate a parameter repeatedly, without manual drawing.

nodes.label: Grid-synchronised vs free-form automation
nodes.blurb: Grid-synchronised automation locks parameter changes to musical timing, while free-form automation moves independently of the grid.

nodes.label: Breakpoint editing
nodes.blurb: Breakpoint editing places individual automation points at precise values, shaping the curve between them by hand.

nodes.label: Clip envelopes
nodes.blurb: Clip envelopes embed automation inside a single clip, controlling its parameters only for that clip's duration.

nodes.label: Compression
nodes.blurb: Compression reduces the gap between a signal's loudest and quietest parts, adding sustain, punch or cohesion.

nodes.label: Gating
nodes.blurb: A gate reduces gain when a signal falls below threshold, removing noise or shaping tight, rhythmic sounds.

nodes.label: Limiting
nodes.blurb: Limiting prevents a signal from exceeding a ceiling, protecting against overload while maximising overall loudness.

nodes.label: Expansion
nodes.blurb: Expansion increases dynamic range rather than reducing it, doing the opposite job to compression.

nodes.label: De-essing
nodes.blurb: De-essing is frequency-specific compression that reduces harsh sibilant 's' and 't' sounds in vocal recordings.

nodes.label: Sidechain compression
nodes.blurb: Sidechain compression triggers gain reduction from one signal, such as a kick, while processing a different target signal.

nodes.label: Threshold & ratio
nodes.blurb: Threshold sets the level compression begins at, while ratio (e.g. 4:1) sets how much gain reduction is applied.

nodes.label: Attack & release
nodes.blurb: Fast attack with slow release smooths a signal; slow attack with fast release preserves the transient punch.

nodes.label: Make-up gain
nodes.blurb: Make-up gain restores level after compression by shifting the whole transfer curve upward, not just the compressed part.

nodes.label: Knee
nodes.blurb: A soft knee compresses gradually around the threshold, while a hard knee applies compression immediately and abruptly.

nodes.label: Gate parameters
nodes.blurb: Hold keeps a gate open for a minimum time after triggering; range sets the reduction when it closes.

nodes.label: Compression & gating graphs
nodes.blurb: Compression and gating are assessed by drawing input/output graphs showing the threshold, curve and knee shape accurately.
nodes.family: Drawing Graphs of Compression and Gating

nodes.label: XY (Coincident pair)
nodes.blurb: XY uses two coincident cardioids at 90–135°, giving excellent mono compatibility but a narrower stereo image.

nodes.label: AB (Spaced pair)
nodes.blurb: AB spaces two omnidirectional mics apart for a wide image, but risks phase cancellation when summed to mono.

nodes.label: ORTF
nodes.blurb: ORTF angles two cardioids at 110° with capsules 17cm apart, balancing stereo width with mono compatibility.

nodes.label: Mid-Side (M-S)
nodes.blurb: Mid-Side combines a cardioid and figure-of-eight mic, letting stereo width be adjusted after recording with perfect mono compatibility.

nodes.label: Blumlein
nodes.blurb: Blumlein pairs two coincident figure-of-eight mics at 90° for natural, full 360° room ambience capture.

nodes.label: Panning conventions
nodes.blurb: Bass, kick and lead vocals are conventionally panned centre, while guitars and keyboards spread across the stereo field.

nodes.label: Audience vs performer perspective
nodes.blurb: Audience perspective is the standard panning convention, describing what the audience hears rather than the performer's view.

nodes.label: Phantom centre
nodes.blurb: Equal signal sent to both speakers creates a phantom centre, an image with no real source between them.

nodes.label: Mono compatibility & phase cancellation
nodes.blurb: Summing a mix to mono reveals phase cancellation, which is why bass is conventionally kept centred and mono.

nodes.label: Haas effect
nodes.blurb: The Haas effect uses a short 1–30ms delay on one channel to create width without an audible echo.

nodes.label: Auto-panning
nodes.blurb: Auto-panning automates a sound's movement across the stereo field, creating rhythmic or spatial interest over time.

nodes.label: Big Mono
nodes.blurb: Big Mono avoids hard-panning every pseudo-stereo source to the extremes, which collapses the mix's sense of space.

nodes.label: ITD / IID
nodes.blurb: Interaural time and intensity differences are the two cues the brain uses to locate sound.

nodes.label: Low & high shelf filters
nodes.blurb: A shelf filter boosts or cuts everything above or below a set frequency, shaping overall brightness or warmth.

nodes.label: High-pass filter
nodes.blurb: A high-pass filter removes frequencies below its cutoff, clearing rumble from almost every track except bass and kick.

nodes.label: Band-pass filter
nodes.blurb: A band-pass filter passes only a narrow frequency window, cutting everything above and below that range.

nodes.label: Parametric & graphic EQ
nodes.blurb: Parametric EQ gives full control over frequency, gain and Q; graphic EQ offers fixed bands for quick shaping.

nodes.label: Gain & cut-off frequency
nodes.blurb: Gain sets how much a frequency is boosted or cut, while cut-off frequency sets where that change begins.

nodes.label: Q (bandwidth)
nodes.blurb: Q sets how wide or narrow a frequency band is, from surgical narrow cuts to broad musical shaping.

nodes.label: Resonance
nodes.blurb: Resonance emphasises frequencies right at the cutoff point, useful for locating ringing, feedback or room-mode problems.

nodes.label: Sibilance correction
nodes.blurb: Harsh 's' and 't' sounds around 5–8kHz are tamed with a narrow-band cut or a dedicated de-esser.

nodes.label: Noise & hum reduction
nodes.blurb: A high-pass filter clears low-frequency rumble, while notch filters target specific noise like 50/60Hz mains hum.

nodes.label: Sweep EQ technique
nodes.blurb: Sweeping a narrow boosted band across the spectrum reveals resonant or problem frequencies before they are cut.

nodes.label: Single & multi-tap delay
nodes.blurb: Single-tap delay produces one repeat per echo; multi-tap gives each repeat its own time, level and pan.

nodes.label: Slapback delay
nodes.blurb: A single fast repeat with no feedback fuses into a doubling rather than an audible echo.

nodes.label: Ping-pong delay
nodes.blurb: Two delay lines with crossed feedback paths bounce repeats alternately between left and right channels.

nodes.label: Tempo-synced delay
nodes.blurb: Delay time locked to song tempo keeps repeats landing precisely on the beat.

nodes.label: Delay time & feedback
nodes.blurb: Delay time sets the gap before the first repeat; feedback routes output back to input for further repeats.

nodes.label: Delay pan & EQ
nodes.blurb: Panning and EQ on delay repeats shape their stereo placement and add tonal darkening across the feedback loop.

nodes.label: Automatic double tracking (ADT)
nodes.blurb: ADT combines a short 15–30ms delay, subtle pitch modulation and hard left/right panning to fake a doubled take.

nodes.label: Tape delay simulation
nodes.blurb: Tape delay sets its time from record-to-playback head spacing, and each repeat grows quieter and tonally darker.

nodes.label: Comb filtering
nodes.blurb: Below roughly 25ms, dry and delayed signal sum and cancel at regular intervals, producing a comb-filtered tone.

nodes.label: Throw delay
nodes.blurb: Throw delay automates the send rather than the return, choosing which words are thrown into the repeat.

nodes.label: Room, hall, chamber & cathedral
nodes.blurb: Room, hall, chamber and cathedral reverbs simulate increasingly large acoustic spaces, each with progressively longer decay times.

nodes.label: Spring & plate reverb
nodes.blurb: Spring reverb adds a twang from vibrating steel springs, while plate reverb gives a dense, bright, non-spatial sound.

nodes.label: Algorithmic reverb
nodes.blurb: Algorithmic reverb synthesises reflections in real time using delay lines and filters, making every parameter fully editable.

nodes.label: Convolution reverb
nodes.blurb: Convolution reverb applies the impulse response of a real space or hardware unit, giving realistic but fixed results.

nodes.label: Hybrid reverb
nodes.blurb: Hybrid reverb blends convolution for early reflections with algorithmic processing for the tail, combining realism with flexibility.

nodes.label: Pre-delay
nodes.blurb: Pre-delay is the gap between direct sound and reverb onset; a longer gap implies a larger space.

nodes.label: Decay time (RT60)
nodes.blurb: RT60 measures how long reverb takes to decay by 60dB, determining the perceived size of a space.

nodes.label: Diffusion & density
nodes.blurb: Diffusion controls how smooth or grainy the reflection pattern sounds, from sparse and grainy to dense and smooth.

nodes.label: Damping
nodes.blurb: Damping sets how quickly high frequencies decay within the tail, producing a darker, warmer character at high settings.

nodes.label: Early reflections
nodes.blurb: Early reflections are the first distinct echoes off nearby surfaces, shaping the perceived size of the room.

nodes.label: Pre-fader & post-fader sends
nodes.blurb: A pre-fader send keeps reverb decaying independently of the fader; a post-fader send makes it follow the fader.

nodes.label: Gated reverb
nodes.blurb: A gate abruptly cuts the reverb tail once the dry signal falls below a set threshold level.

nodes.label: Reverse reverb
nodes.blurb: A reversed reverb tail placed before the dry sound creates a rising swell that builds into the note.

nodes.label: Ducked reverb
nodes.blurb: Side-chain compression reduces reverb level while the dry source plays, keeping the mix clear without losing depth.

nodes.label: LFO (rate, depth & waveform)
nodes.blurb: An LFO's rate, depth and waveform set how fast, how strongly and how a parameter is modulated.

nodes.label: Chorus
nodes.blurb: Chorus duplicates the signal and modulates a 20–50ms delay with an LFO, creating a thickening, multi-voice shimmer.

nodes.label: Flanger
nodes.blurb: Flanger uses a much shorter 1–10ms delay with feedback than chorus, producing a sweeping, metallic comb-filtered sound.

nodes.label: Phaser
nodes.blurb: Phaser splits the signal through allpass filters whose LFO-swept phase shifts create smoothly sweeping, non-harmonic notches.

nodes.label: Tremolo
nodes.blurb: Tremolo uses an LFO to cyclically vary amplitude, producing a pulsing volume change rather than any pitch shift.

nodes.label: Vibrato
nodes.blurb: Vibrato uses an LFO to cyclically vary pitch, producing a wavering pitch change rather than any volume shift.

nodes.label: Ring modulation
nodes.blurb: Ring modulation multiplies carrier and modulator signals together, generating new sum-and-difference frequencies for metallic, bell-like tones.

nodes.label: Carrier & modulator
nodes.blurb: The carrier is the signal being modulated, while the modulator, usually an LFO, controls how it changes.

nodes.label: Overdrive
nodes.blurb: Overdrive mimics a gently pushed tube amp with soft clipping, preserving the instrument's tone and dynamic responsiveness.

nodes.label: Fuzz
nodes.blurb: Fuzz applies extreme clipping close to a square wave, producing heavy odd-harmonic content and a vintage, psychedelic character.

nodes.label: Saturation
nodes.blurb: Saturation adds subtle harmonic warmth emulating analogue tape, valve or transformer circuits without audibly clipping the waveform.

nodes.label: Bitcrushing
nodes.blurb: Bitcrushing reduces bit depth and sample rate, adding quantisation noise and aliasing artefacts for a lo-fi digital character.

nodes.label: Drive & tone
nodes.blurb: Drive pushes the signal into its nonlinear range before distortion, while tone shapes brightness afterwards through filtering.

nodes.label: Hard vs soft clipping
nodes.blurb: Hard clipping abruptly truncates peaks for an aggressive tone; soft clipping compresses them gradually for a smoother character.

nodes.label: Symmetrical & asymmetrical clipping
nodes.blurb: Symmetrical clipping cuts both peaks equally, producing odd harmonics only; asymmetrical clipping cuts unevenly, adding even harmonics.

nodes.label: Even vs odd harmonics
nodes.blurb: Even harmonics sound warmer and more consonant, linked to tube distortion; odd harmonics sound more dissonant and aggressive.

nodes.label: Peak vs RMS level
nodes.blurb: Distortion raises RMS level relative to peak, because clipping increases average signal energy while the peak stays fixed.

nodes.label: Tube vs transistor distortion
nodes.blurb: Tube distortion adds natural compression and even-harmonic warmth, while transistor distortion clips more tightly with predominantly odd harmonics.

nodes.label: Waveshaping
nodes.blurb: Waveshaping reshapes a waveform using a mathematical transfer function, the basis of digital distortion and saturation processing.

nodes.label: Gain staging & headroom
nodes.blurb: Careful gain staging maintains headroom below 0dBFS through the signal chain, preventing unintended digital clipping.

nodes.label: Fader balancing
nodes.blurb: Setting relative fader levels puts vocals and drums forward while supporting instruments stay musically subordinate.

nodes.label: Fader automation
nodes.blurb: Automating fader moves keeps balance appropriate as a track shifts, for example from verse into chorus.

nodes.label: Headroom
nodes.blurb: Leaving headroom below 0 dBFS gives a safety margin against clipping when setting mix levels.

nodes.label: Panning & stereo placement
nodes.blurb: Positioning elements across the stereo field creates separation and width between instruments and voices.

nodes.label: Mono compatibility check
nodes.blurb: Checking a mix in mono reveals panning-dependent masking and phase issues that stereo playback hides.

nodes.label: Frequency masking
nodes.blurb: Two instruments sharing a frequency region obscure each other unless EQ or arrangement resolves the clash.

nodes.label: Making space (EQ)
nodes.blurb: Cutting a conflicting frequency in one instrument, rather than boosting the other, clears space without changing its tone.

nodes.label: Depth via reverb & delay
nodes.blurb: Time-based effects place elements at different perceived distances, building blend and cohesion in a mix.

nodes.label: Creative vs technical balance
nodes.blurb: Technically correct balance avoids clipping, but musically appropriate balance prioritises elements by genre and intent.

nodes.label: Static mix principle
nodes.blurb: Building a rough balance from faders alone before processing reveals arrangement hierarchy and exposes masking early.

nodes.label: Monitoring for mixing
nodes.blurb: Accurate balance judgements depend on an appropriate monitoring level and listening environment.

nodes.label: Headphones vs loudspeakers
nodes.blurb: A mix balanced on headphones may not translate to loudspeakers, so engineers check across playback systems.

nodes.label: Purpose of mastering
nodes.blurb: Mastering is the final post-production stage, preparing a mix for distribution and consistency across an album.

nodes.label: Mastering signal chain
nodes.blurb: The mastering chain runs EQ, compression, multiband compression, stereo enhancement, limiting, then dithering in that order.

nodes.label: LUFS & loudness targets
nodes.blurb: LUFS measures perceived loudness, and streaming platforms and broadcast each enforce different integrated loudness targets.

nodes.label: True peak & intersample peaks
nodes.blurb: True peak metering catches intersample peaks that standard peak meters miss, so limiters use a dBTP ceiling.

nodes.label: Loudness war & dynamic range
nodes.blurb: Pushing loudness through heavy limiting sacrifices dynamic range, a trade-off known as the loudness war.

nodes.label: Loudness normalisation
nodes.blurb: Streaming platforms turn down over-limited masters to a target level, removing the commercial advantage of loud mastering.

nodes.label: Brickwall limiting
nodes.blurb: A limiter sets a hard ceiling near the top of the signal, maximising loudness without clipping.

nodes.label: Mastering EQ
nodes.blurb: Subtle corrective EQ removes sub-sonic content and matches tonal balance across an album rather than reshaping individual sounds.

nodes.label: Glue compression
nodes.blurb: Low-ratio bus compression with long attack and release times adds cohesion across the whole mix.

nodes.label: Multiband compression
nodes.blurb: Splitting the signal into frequency bands lets one problem region be controlled without affecting the full mix.

nodes.label: Mid-side processing
nodes.blurb: Encoding a mix into mid and side channels lets stereo width be adjusted independently of centred elements.

nodes.label: Bass mono compatibility
nodes.blurb: Summing low frequencies to mono prevents phase cancellation when a master is played on a mono system.

nodes.label: Dithering
nodes.blurb: Adding low-level noise once during bit-depth reduction masks the quantisation distortion caused by discarding bits.

nodes.label: Format & delivery prep
nodes.blurb: Final masters export as WAV, AIFF, FLAC or MP3, matched to the platform's sample rate and bit depth.

nodes.label: RT60 (reverberation time)
nodes.blurb: RT60 measures how long reverb takes to decay by 60 dB, growing with room size and less absorption.

nodes.label: Direct-to-reverberant (R/D) ratio
nodes.blurb: The ratio of reverberated to direct sound tells a listener how far away a sound source seems.

nodes.label: Standing waves (room modes)
nodes.blurb: Low frequencies build up between parallel walls in small rooms, causing uneven bass at different listening positions.

nodes.label: Absorption vs diffusion
nodes.blurb: Absorption converts sound energy to heat while diffusion scatters reflections, and both reduce problems in different ways.

nodes.label: Drivers (woofer & tweeter)
nodes.blurb: Woofers reproduce low frequencies and tweeters reproduce high frequencies, sometimes split further by a mid-range driver.

nodes.label: Crossover networks
nodes.blurb: A crossover splits the incoming signal into frequency bands and routes each band to the correct driver.

nodes.label: Bass reflex ports
nodes.blurb: A tuned port extends low-frequency response by channelling rear woofer radiation, trading extension for tightness.

nodes.label: Nearfield monitors
nodes.blurb: Positioned 1-2 m from the listener, nearfield monitors let direct sound dominate over room reflections.

nodes.label: Midfield & farfield monitors
nodes.blurb: Midfield and soffit-mounted farfield monitors sit further from the listener and suit larger professional control rooms.

nodes.label: Active vs passive monitors
nodes.blurb: Active monitors carry built-in amplification per driver, while passive monitors need an external amplifier and passive crossover.

nodes.label: Flat frequency response
nodes.blurb: Studio monitors aim to reproduce all frequencies equally so mixing decisions are not skewed by added colouration.

nodes.label: Consumer speaker colouration
nodes.blurb: Consumer speakers boost bass and treble to flatter recordings, unlike monitors, which should be trusted uncompensated.

nodes.label: Small speaker limitations
nodes.blurb: Mobile phones and laptop speakers cannot reproduce low frequencies, so mixes must survive without relying on sub-bass.

nodes.label: Equilateral triangle placement
nodes.blurb: Positioning monitors and listener as an equilateral triangle with tweeters at ear height keeps stereo imaging accurate.

nodes.label: Boundary effects & isolation
nodes.blurb: Placing monitors too close to walls builds up bass, so isolation pads and distance keep response accurate.

nodes.label: Reference monitoring
nodes.blurb: Checking a mix on multiple speaker types, including consumer systems, reveals how it will translate across playback devices.

nodes.label: Headphone monitoring
nodes.blurb: Headphones offer isolation and detail but lack crossfeed, which exaggerates the stereo image compared with speakers.

nodes.label: Subwoofers
nodes.blurb: Adding a subwoofer extends low-frequency monitoring where small monitors cannot reproduce sub-bass content.

nodes.label: Balanced connections
nodes.blurb: Two conductors carry the signal in opposite polarity, so induced noise cancels out via common-mode rejection.

nodes.label: TRS vs TS jacks
nodes.blurb: A TRS jack's two insulating bands can mean balanced mono or unbalanced stereo, depending on the equipment.

nodes.label: XLR pin assignment
nodes.blurb: Pin 1 is ground, pin 2 carries the hot signal, and pin 3 carries the cold.

nodes.label: DI box
nodes.blurb: A DI box converts a high-impedance instrument signal to balanced low-impedance XLR, enabling long cable runs without noise.

nodes.label: Active vs passive DI
nodes.blurb: Active DI suits passive pickups like guitar; passive DI suits already-active sources such as keyboards.

nodes.label: Common-mode rejection
nodes.blurb: Noise induced identically on both conductors cancels when the cold wire's polarity is flipped back at the input.

nodes.label: Signal levels
nodes.blurb: Mic, instrument and line level differ by tens of decibels, so mismatched gear sounds too quiet or overloads.

nodes.label: Analogue vs digital signals
nodes.blurb: Analogue signals vary continuously in amplitude; digital signals store discrete binary values, trading warmth for precision.

nodes.label: ADC and DAC
nodes.blurb: An ADC converts an analogue waveform into digital samples; a DAC reverses this at the monitoring stage.

nodes.label: Sampling and sample rate
nodes.blurb: Sample rate is how often amplitude is measured per second; higher rates capture faster, higher-frequency changes.

nodes.label: Quantisation
nodes.blurb: Each sampled amplitude is rounded to the nearest value the bit depth allows, creating quantisation error.

nodes.label: Nyquist theorem
nodes.blurb: Sample rate must be at least twice the highest frequency captured, so 44.1 kHz covers human hearing.

nodes.label: Aliasing
nodes.blurb: Frequencies above the Nyquist limit fold back as artefacts unless an anti-aliasing filter removes them first.

nodes.label: Bit depth
nodes.blurb: Bit depth sets how many amplitude values each sample can take, so higher depths measure more precisely.

nodes.label: Dynamic range
nodes.blurb: More bits per sample mean a wider dynamic range, so 24-bit captures quieter and louder detail than 16-bit.

nodes.label: File size calculations
nodes.blurb: File size scales with sample rate, bit depth, channel count and duration, so higher quality means more storage.

nodes.label: Analogue characteristics
nodes.blurb: Tape wear and component ageing degrade analogue signal quality, though some prize the added harmonic warmth.

nodes.label: Digital audio advantages
nodes.blurb: Digital copies are bit-perfect with zero generation loss, enabling sample-accurate editing and precise recall of settings.

nodes.label: Recording signal chain
nodes.blurb: A recording signal passes microphone, ADC, DAW processing, DAC, then monitors, converting form twice along the way.

nodes.label: Frequency and period maths
nodes.blurb: Frequency and period are reciprocals, so converting between hertz and milliseconds is a core exam-tested skill.

nodes.label: Octave doubling and halving
nodes.blurb: Moving an octave up doubles frequency and halves the period; moving down does the reverse.

nodes.label: Semitone and cents maths
nodes.blurb: Equal-temperament semitone ratios and cents give precise fine-tuning calculations for synthesis and pitch-correction work.

nodes.label: Sample rate and Nyquist maths
nodes.blurb: Calculating the minimum sample rate for a given frequency range is a recurring exam question type.

nodes.label: Dynamic range calculations
nodes.blurb: Bit depth determines available dynamic range, a standard calculation comparing 16-bit and 24-bit recording.

nodes.label: BPM to delay-time maths
nodes.blurb: Converting tempo in beats per minute to millisecond delay times keeps synced repeats locked to the groove.

nodes.label: Note-value and grid maths
nodes.blurb: Time-signature and note-value relationships let you quantise recordings precisely to the musical grid.

nodes.label: dB scale and ratios
nodes.blurb: The decibel scale is logarithmic, so equal steps represent equal ratios rather than equal amounts.

nodes.label: Gain staging calculations
nodes.blurb: Working out optimal levels at each stage of the signal chain avoids both clipping and noise.

nodes.label: Compression ratio maths
nodes.blurb: Comparing input and output levels against the ratio setting predicts how hard a compressor squashes a signal.

nodes.label: Filter slope maths
nodes.blurb: Filter slope in dB per octave measures attenuation rate, not the cutoff frequency, a common exam trap.

nodes.label: RMS vs peak maths
nodes.blurb: Level-matching a distorted signal at its peak still raises RMS, because clipping squashes the waveform flatter.

nodes.label: Signal level types
nodes.blurb: Mic, line and instrument signals sit at different voltages, so connecting mismatched stages causes noise or overload.

nodes.label: The decibel scale
nodes.blurb: Decibels express a ratio, not an absolute value, on a logarithmic scale matched to human hearing.

nodes.label: dBu, dBV and dBFS
nodes.blurb: Professional gear references 0 dBu, consumer gear 0 dBV, and digital systems 0 dBFS as their absolute ceiling.

nodes.label: Peak metering
nodes.blurb: Peak meters catch the instantaneous maximum level, making them essential for preventing digital clipping.

nodes.label: RMS metering
nodes.blurb: RMS meters average signal power over time, reflecting perceived loudness but missing fast transient peaks.

nodes.label: VU metering
nodes.blurb: VU meters show average level with slow ballistics, useful for consistent gain staging on analogue gear.

nodes.label: PPM metering
nodes.blurb: PPM meters respond faster than VU, catching peaks more reliably, and are the broadcast industry standard.

nodes.label: LUFS and loudness metering
nodes.blurb: LUFS measures perceived loudness for streaming and broadcast, weighted to match human hearing sensitivity.

nodes.label: Gain staging
nodes.blurb: Setting correct levels at every stage of the chain keeps a signal clean without clipping or noise.

nodes.label: Clipping and distortion
nodes.blurb: Digital clipping cuts a signal abruptly at 0 dBFS, while analogue clipping compresses peaks more gradually.

nodes.label: Noise floor and SNR
nodes.blurb: Signal-to-noise ratio measures how far the signal sits above the system's background noise floor.
